newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine power struggle holds reform hostage.
newsitem.headline: Argentine power struggle holds reform hostage.

text.p: Argentina's reform plans for 1997 are being held hostage by a war of wills between President Carlos Menem and Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, the man bent on taking his place in 1999.
The 66-year-old president is determined to keep his grip on the Peronist Party until "the last day, the last hour and the last minute of my mandate."

Meanwhile, Duhalde, who stepped down as Menem's vice president to run for governor of Buenos Aires province, is using his powerful political base to make certain Menem does not thwart his ambitions for 1999 by seeking a third consecutive term in office.

Menem has said the talk of his "re-re-election," which surfaced almost as soon as he won a second term in May 1995, is farcical. He notes that his daughter Zulemita is opposed to him running in 1999. And almost as an after-thought, he points out that the Argentine constitution rules out a third consecutive term.

Still, a subtle test of wills between the two men will likely influence progress on pending reforms, such as labor legislation and the privatization of airports, post office and mortage lender Banco Hipotecario, in the run-up to midterm elections in October, analysts said. The contest could then flare into open political warfare ahead of 1999.

"For me, this is Argentina's biggest political problem," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Raul Buonnuome. "Menem doesn't want his power to deteriorate in his last two years in office, and Duhalde wants to launch his campaign."
Menem secured constitutional reforms in 1994 that allowed him seek re-election, but he cannot run for a third term until 2003.

Nevertheless, Duhalde sees danger signals in the "Menem 99" posters that regularly appear at party conferences and in a Senate bill proposed by a Menem loyalist that would allow referendums. The measure is widely seen as a first step in changing the constitution again, this time by plebiscite.

"The president is not more important than the constitution," Duhalde said, adamant not to sacrifice his own ambitions to Menem's, as he did for the last election. Duhalde was Menem's running mate in 1989.
The Peronist ranks are splitting just when the party should be uniting to fight a difficult election against the Radical and Frepaso parties, which both lead the governing party in opinion polls.

"It's an important issue because there is obviously a struggle to position themselves for power. This is making itself felt in the lack of progress on important laws in Congress," said independent economist Pedro Lacoste.
"I think it's going to be a very complicated year for politics with very limited progress on reforms," he said.
"If the capital markets and the real economy were not in the shape they are in, this conflict would have unsuspected repercussions," said consultants Melconian y Santangelo.

Duhalde, whose province is home to 40 percent of the Argentine population, controls 37 of the 130-strong Peronist majority in the 257-seat Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress. Menem only has about 20 ultra-loyalists there.
Duhalde also has the CGT union federation in his camp. Once loyal to Menem, the federation is up in arms over proposed labor reforms.
While the party tries to present a united front ahead of the midterm elections, with 127 seats at stake, Duhalde's allies are already preparing for the 1999 campaign.

Sen. Antonio Cafiero, a government minister in the 1950s under party founder Juan Peron, lobbied for primaries to choose the 1999 candidate, "to help Duhalde change policy, because we see huge sectors of society suffering the consequences of austerity..."

Duhalde has argued that a third Menem term would mark a setback "on the road to modernity," though the governor has failed to convince business leaders that he would wholeheartedly embrace reform if elected president. That is one possible reason Argentine businessmen have not opposed Menem seeking "re-re-election."

"These clashes are about fundamental differences in their vision for Argentina towards 1999," said Buonnuome. "Duhalde's position on structural reform is not clear, raising doubts about his commitment to deepen reforms."
